blocks.content: The story starts with a simple question that needs an answer right now.

Your order service just received a payment. Before it can confirm the order, it needs to know: does inventory have the item in stock? It can't proceed without the answer. It can't queue the question and move on. It needs to ask, wait, and act on the response all in sequence.
This is synchronous communication. One service calls another, waits for the response, and uses that response to continue. The caller is blocked until the callee replies.

Most of the requests you make every day are synchronous. When you load a webpage, your browser waits for the server. When a payment service calls a fraud detection service, it waits for the verdict. When you run a database query, your code waits for rows.
Synchronous communication is the default mental model of how services talk and understanding its properties, failure modes, and limits is essential to designing systems that hold up under load.
1. What synchronous actually means
Synchronous communication has three defining properties:

["The caller blocks. While waiting for the response, the calling service cannot do other work on that thread or goroutine. Resources are held open.
","The response is immediate. The callee processes the request and returns a response in the same connection, before the caller moves on.
","Tight temporal coupling. Both services must be available at the same moment. If the callee is down, the call fails immediately.
"]
items: The caller blocks. While waiting for the response, the calling service cannot do other work on that thread or goroutine. Resources are held open.
The response is immediate. The callee processes the request and returns a response in the same connection, before the caller moves on.
Tight temporal coupling. Both services must be available at the same moment. If the callee is down, the call fails immediately.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278083517-392327350.png
blocks.alt: Service A blocks waiting on Service B, then resumes on response

blocks.content: While doing its work, Service A needs inventory information and sends an HTTP request (GET /inventory/item-42) to Service B. After sending the request, Service A cannot continue its work because it depends on the response from Service B.

Service B receives the request and queries its database to determine whether the item is in stock. During this entire time, Service A is blocked and simply waits for the response. Its thread is occupied even though it is not doing any useful work.

Once Service B finishes processing and returns { in_stock: true }, the response reaches Service A and it resumes its execution. This waiting behavior is the key characteristic of synchronous communication the caller cannot proceed until the callee finishes and sends back a response.

The critical implication: latency compounds. If Service A calls B, C, and D sequentially, the total latency is the sum. If each takes 50ms, the request takes 150ms minimum before A does any work of its own. In a chain of five microservices each taking 30ms, the user waits 150ms just in network time.
2. The two dominant protocols

Most synchronous communication between services happens using two protocols: HTTP/REST and gRPC. Both follow the request-response model, but they make different trade-offs in performance, tooling, and developer experience.
1. HTTP/REST
The universal default. Service A makes an HTTP request to Service B's endpoint. B processes it and returns an HTTP response.

GET  /inventory/items/42          → check stock
POST /payments/charge             → process payment
PUT  /orders/123/status           → update order status

blocks.content: Why it's the default: works everywhere, cacheable, human-readable, massive tooling ecosystem, every language has HTTP clients, easy to debug with curl.
The cost: text-based (JSON adds serialisation overhead), HTTP/1.1 has one request per connection, no built-in streaming for most implementations.
2. gRPC
Binary protocol over HTTP/2. Services define contracts in .proto files. Code is generated for both client and server. Communication is over typed binary messages, multiplexed on a single connection.
Why to use it: 3–10× smaller payload than JSON, faster serialisation, HTTP/2 multiplexing means many calls share one connection, type safety enforced at compile time, supports streaming natively.
The cost: binary is not human-readable, harder to debug, browser support requires a proxy layer.
The pattern at scale: REST at the external boundary (developers expect it, CDN can cache it), gRPC internally between services (performance, type safety, streaming).
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 3. Failure modes
Synchronous communication introduces a specific class of failures that don't exist in asynchronous systems.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278085612-364044584.png
blocks.alt: A slow Service C cascades thread exhaustion up through B and A

blocks.content: cascading failure in a synchronous system.

Everything starts with Service C. Normally, it responds in 50ms, but due to a slow database query it suddenly starts taking 8 seconds per request. Since Service B depends on Service C synchronously, every request coming into Service B now waits for those 8 seconds.
As more requests arrive, the threads in Service B become blocked waiting for Service C. Eventually all of B's threads are occupied, and it cannot process any new requests.
Now Service A starts calling Service B. But because B has no free threads left, A also starts waiting. Its threads begin piling up as well. After some time, all of A's threads are blocked too.

At this point, none of the services are actually crashed, but the entire request chain is effectively down because every thread is waiting on another service. A single slow database in Service C has caused thread exhaustion in B, which then caused thread exhaustion in A.

This is the biggest danger of synchronous communication: a problem in one downstream service can propagate upstream and make multiple healthy services unavailable. This chain reaction is called a cascading failure.
4. The 3 Defences
Synchronous systems are vulnerable to cascading failures, so every service should protect itself with timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers.
blocks.text: Synchronous systems are vulnerable to cascading failures, so every service should protect itself with timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers.

blocks.content: 1. Timeouts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278087278-126799834.png
blocks.alt: A timeout aborts a call that does not respond in time

blocks.content: Every synchronous call should have a timeout. If the downstream service does not respond within a fixed time, stop waiting and return an error.
Without timeouts, threads remain blocked and eventually the service runs out of threads.
The request waits for at most 500ms. If the response does not arrive in time, the request fails immediately and the thread becomes available to handle other requests.
2. Retries with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
blocks.text: 2. Retries with Exponential Backoff and Jitter

blocks.content: Some failures are temporary, such as network glitches or brief overloads. Retrying can recover from these failures.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028051-461969293.png
blocks.alt: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter until success

blocks.content: The delay between retries increases exponentially, and a small random delay (jitter) is added so that all clients do not retry at the same moment.
The first retry waits about one second, the second waits about two seconds, and the third waits about four seconds.
Jitter spreads retries over time and prevents thousands of clients from retrying simultaneously and overwhelming the recovering service.
3. Circuit Breaker
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278090607-465522210.png
blocks.alt: Circuit breaker states: closed, open, half open

blocks.content: A circuit breaker monitors failures to a downstream service.
If too many requests fail, the circuit opens and immediately rejects new requests instead of sending them to the failing service.
After a delay, a few test requests are allowed. If they succeed, the circuit closes again

["CLOSED: Everything is healthy. All requests go to the downstream service.
","OPEN: Too many failures occurred. Requests fail immediately without contacting the downstream service.
","HALF-OPEN: small number of test requests are allowed through. If they succeed, the circuit closes. If they fail, it opens again.
"]
items: CLOSED: Everything is healthy. All requests go to the downstream service.
OPEN: Too many failures occurred. Requests fail immediately without contacting the downstream service.
HALF-OPEN: small number of test requests are allowed through. If they succeed, the circuit closes. If they fail, it opens again.

blocks.content: The circuit breaker prevents thread exhaustion and stops one failing service from bringing down the entire system.
4. Using All Three Together
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028045-78499583.png
blocks.alt: Timeout, retry, and circuit breaker layered around a downstream call

blocks.content: ["Timeout prevents waiting forever.","Retry recovers from temporary failures.","Circuit Breaker prevents cascading failures."]
These three patterns together form the foundation of resilient synchronous communication in distributed systems.
5. Circuit breaker In synchronous communication.

A circuit breaker tracks the error rate of calls to a downstream service. When the error rate exceeds a threshold, it "opens" immediately returning an error without even attempting the call, protecting both the caller's threads and the struggling downstream from additional load.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278094010-2983409.png
blocks.alt: An open circuit fails fast instead of calling the downstream service

blocks.content: Circuit breakers are the most important resilience pattern for synchronous communication.
Without them, a failing downstream causes every caller to wait out the full timeout before failing exhausting threads.
With a circuit breaker open, callers fail in microseconds, freeing their threads immediately and allowing them to serve other requests or return graceful degraded responses.
6. Sequential vs parallel calls
When a service needs data from multiple downstreams, sequential calls are the obvious first implementation and the wrong one for independent calls.
1. Sequential: total time = 80 + 60 + 40 = 180ms

user    = user_service.get(user_id)        # 80ms
orders  = order_service.get(user_id)       # 60ms
prefs   = prefs_service.get(user_id)       # 40ms

blocks.content: When calls are independent (the result of one doesn't determine the input to another), parallelize them. The latency becomes the slowest call rather than the sum. At four downstream calls averaging 50ms each, this is the difference between 200ms and 50ms response time.
When calls are dependent (you need the user ID from the user service to pass to the order service), they must be sequential but that's a data dependency, not a design choice.
7. Service mesh

In a microservices system with dozens of services all making synchronous calls to each other, you'd have to implement timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, mTLS, and distributed tracing in every service.
A service mesh moves all of this out of application code.
A sidecar proxy (Envoy) runs alongside each service. All inbound and outbound traffic goes through it.
The mesh handles retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, load balancing, mutual TLS, and emits telemetry automatically, for every service, with no application code changes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278095673-691442177.png
blocks.alt: A service mesh sidecar proxy handles cross cutting concerns

blocks.content: Istio and AWS App Mesh are the common implementations. The application sees a simple local call; the mesh handles the complexity.
8. When synchronous is right and when it isn't
blocks.text: 8. When synchronous is right and when it isn't

blocks.content: Use synchronous when:

["You need the answer before you can proceed (inventory check before confirming order)","The operation must be consistent the response confirms the action succeeded","The user is waiting and expects an immediate response","Latency is within acceptable bounds end to end"]
items: You need the answer before you can proceed (inventory check before confirming order)
The operation must be consistent the response confirms the action succeeded
The user is waiting and expects an immediate response
Latency is within acceptable bounds end to end

blocks.content: Switch to async when:

["You don't need the result to continue (send a confirmation email after placing order)","The operation takes seconds or minutes (video encoding, report generation)","The downstream is unreliable and you can tolerate eventual consistency","You want to absorb traffic spikes without back-pressure on the caller","You're building an event-driven system where decoupling matters more than immediacy"]
items: You don't need the result to continue (send a confirmation email after placing order)
The operation takes seconds or minutes (video encoding, report generation)
The downstream is unreliable and you can tolerate eventual consistency
You want to absorb traffic spikes without back-pressure on the caller
You're building an event-driven system where decoupling matters more than immediacy

blocks.content: The mistake teams make: defaulting to synchronous for everything because it's the simpler mental model, then finding that one slow downstream service brings down unrelated parts of the system.
The opposite mistake: making everything async to avoid coupling, then losing the immediate consistency guarantees the product actually requires.
9. HLD interview ( How to talk about this )
blocks.text: 9. HLD interview ( How to talk about this )

blocks.content: When drawing a microservices architecture, every arrow between services is a synchronous call. The interviewer wants to see that you understand what those arrows mean.

Name the trade-off: Synchronous communication gives us immediate consistency and a simple programming model the caller knows the result before moving on. The cost is temporal coupling: both services must be available simultaneously, and the caller's latency is bounded below by the callee's latency.

Talk about cascades: The main danger in a synchronous chain is cascading failure. If the inventory service slows to 8 seconds, the order service's threads fill up waiting for it, and the API gateway's threads fill up waiting for the order service. I'd put timeouts, retries with jitter, and circuit breakers on every synchronous call to prevent this.

Distinguish sequential from parallel: When building the product detail page that needs user data, pricing, and inventory, I'd make those three calls in parallel since they're independent. Sequential adds those latencies; parallel takes the max.

Show you know when to switch: The order confirmation email doesn't need to be synchronous the user doesn't need to wait for it. I'd publish an event after the order is confirmed and let the notification service consume it asynchronously. If the email service is down, the order still completes we just retry the email later.

Name the tools: For service-to-service calls internally I'd use gRPC binary, typed, HTTP/2 multiplexing, native streaming. For the public API, REST. For cross-cutting concerns like circuit breaking and mTLS across all services, I'd use a service mesh rather than implementing it in every service individually.
